anthropology.label: Anthropology & ethnography
anthropology.description: Ethnographic observation, comparison, historical reconstruction and interpretation generate different accounts of social life. Exchanges with historians involve particular works and methods; colonial knowledge, research authority and the representation of cultures are contested within and beyond the discipline.
anthropology.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct stages include Tylor and Frazer, Boasian historical particularism, and later interpretive anthropology associated with Geertz. These do not form one continuous theory.

representative_people.context: Studies acquired culture through comparative stages and survivals; the hierarchy is his proposition, not the atlas’s classification of peoples.

anthropology.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

biography.label: Biography / life writing
biography.date_label: Ancient roots · Strachey 1918 · Davis 1995 · crosses fields
biography.description: Uses individual and collective lives to ask historical questions about character, social relations, power and experience. Documentary reconstruction, psychoanalytic interpretation, contextual comparison and relational trajectories pose different problems. Authors, subjects, editors and collaborators shape the surviving account.
biography.representative_figures_and_works: Ancient roots; Carlyle’s On Heroes (1841) is one nineteenth-century strand, not its sole foundation. Strachey (1918); Erikson (1958); Davis (1995).

representative_people.context: The opening Heroes lecture gives creative individuals and practical belief a large explanatory role. This is one nineteenth-century strand, not biography’s origin or all Carlyle’s historical writing.
representative_people.works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening (5 May 1840)

representative_people.context: Selects compact portraits using French eloges models and existing biographies. Woolf later praises one royal biography while criticizing another; neither authorial impartiality nor a uniform critical verdict is assumed.

biography.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

strands.title: Labour lives and collective authorship
strands.focus: Torr’s Mann project draws on biographical materials and collaborative preparation. The incomplete continuation, manuscript/publication distinction and Murphy’s criticism make the production of a life history visible.
strands.works: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956); further fragments edited by E. P. Thompson, Our History 26–27 (1962)

strands.title: Individual reconstruction and social explanation
strands.focus: Power pairs lives with estate books, letters, household advice and material remains. Her personal treatment is a teaching method; Postan’s later reconstruction makes editorial mediation visible.

strands.title: Biographical sympathy and revision through evidence
strands.focus: Wedgwood’s two Strafford treatments offer a case of reassessment through new sources and scholarship. Woolrych’s criticism of eulogy remains visible alongside his appreciation.
strands.works: Strafford (1935); Thomas Wentworth ... A Revaluation (1961); Woolrych memoir (1998)

strands.title: A life as narrative vehicle: reach and missing evidence
strands.focus: Tuchman selects Coucy to travel across a turbulent period but acknowledges documentary limits. Stone questions whether that organizing device yields a sufficiently understood person or explains wider institutions.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), foreword; Stone review (1978)

strands.title: Whose lives and which particulars?
strands.focus: Johnson’s private lives, Brown’s collective recovery and Woolf’s changed criteria show different arguments about biographical significance. They are not a single progression from great men to ordinary people.
strands.works: Rambler 60 (1750); The Black Man (1863); The Art of Biography (1939)

strands.title: Narrated unity and relational trajectories
strands.focus: Bourdieu asks how institutions, interviews and retrospective storytelling produce coherent selves, and proposes trajectories within changing fields. Life history remains possible under relational scrutiny.

strands.title: Scale, norms and bounded agency
strands.focus: Levi distinguishes several uses of lives and locates choices within conflicting norms. Group coherence becomes a question to investigate, not an automatic starting assumption.

strands.title: Contextual reconstruction and its limits
strands.focus: Roche’s Ménétra and Venturi’s Diderot illustrate different contextual procedures in Levi’s account. Context can illuminate gaps while itself requiring a dynamic explanation.
strands.works: Journal de ma vie (1982); Jeunesse de Diderot (1939), mediated by Levi (1989)

strands.title: Comparative lives, religion and colonial power
strands.focus: Davis holds similarities and differences together, tests her categories through an imagined prologue and rejects a single progressive sequence. Marginality does not prevent participation in colonial domination.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995), selected primary passages

strands.title: Publishing, translating and cutting a life record
strands.focus: Davis compares Glikl editions with different treatment of stories and moral commentary. Pappenheim’s role as translator is distinguished from the clinical narrative about her.

strands.title: Teaching, source discovery and collaborative work
strands.focus: Davis names course development, source suggestions, translation, archives, libraries and editing as resources. A selective roster does not exhaust the acknowledged labor behind the book.

strands.title: Psychoanalytic interpretation and critical limits
strands.focus: Erikson’s 1970 retrospective supplies a primary account of his Luther interpretation, while the original 1958 book remains unread. Levi’s generic psychobiography judgment is not an Erikson-specific rebuttal.
strands.works: Young Man Luther (1958); Levi (1989), methodological discussion; Erikson, Autobiographic Notes (1970), p. 750

strands.title: Individual life and historical surroundings
strands.focus: Dilthey’s biographical work and later reflections join individual initiative to institutions and cultural systems. Biography brings contextual factors into view that recollection alone may not supply.
strands.works: Leben Schleiermachers I (1870), through scholarly discussion

strands.title: Psychological motives and limits of inference
strands.focus: Namier argues that professed reasons may conceal unconscious processes, but insists that psychological origins alone do not refute an argument. His warning about fragmentary evidence limits the use of psychological explanations in historical lives.

culture.label: New cultural history
culture.description: Meaning, symbols, rituals, representation, and practices help constitute social life. Draws on anthropology and multiple historical traditions.
culture.representative_figures_and_works: Natalie Zemon Davis; Lynn Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989), whose “Models for Cultural History” are Foucault (O’Brien), Thompson and Davis (Desan), Geertz (Biersack), and White and LaCapra (Kramer).

representative_people.context: Class is a historical relationship formed through material experience and culture; the Making preface explicitly restricts its study to English developments.

representative_people.context: Festive misrule and religious riot read as culturally patterned action, with anthropology used for questions tested on historical evidence (1971–75). Hunt’s 1989 volume makes ‘Thompson and Davis’ a model for cultural history in Desan’s chapter.

representative_people.context: An anthropological resource, not a historian’s membership in a school.

philhistory.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
philhistory.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
philhistory.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
philhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

representative_people.context: Connects everyday inquiry, social memory and changing interpretation while retaining critical checks.
representative_people.works: Everyman His Own Historian (address 1931; publication 1932)

representative_people.context: Proposes testable laws and initial conditions, allowing probability and incomplete explanation sketches.
representative_people.works: The Function of General Laws in History (1942)

representative_people.context: Challenges reducing all historical explanations to a covering-law model; rational action and pragmatic questions are distinct concerns.
representative_people.works: Laws and Explanation in History (1957)

representative_people.context: Treats selection, interpretation and research as reciprocal while rejecting equal validity for every account.
representative_people.works: What Is History? (1961)

representative_people.context: Addresses research, imagination, writing and teaching; Mink cites his insistence on immersion in a period.

representative_people.context: Examines how historical discourse constructs signification and claims reference. Historians’ engagement includes productive use and criticism, not one settled verdict on evidence.

representative_people.context: Asks how source survival and artistic forms shape historical perception.
representative_people.works: The Waning of the Middle Ages (1924), preface and chapter XIX opening

representative_people.context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
representative_people.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Source search, criticism and interpretation cooperate. Material remains, accounts and monuments are not interchangeable; neither authentic documents nor individual intentions alone yield a complete historical explanation.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted Andrews English 1893), §§1–11, 20–24, 28–41

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory and History of Historiography (Italian 1917; consulted 1921 Ainslie translation from 1919 edition), I.1

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception through Skinner; The Idea of History (1946, posthumous), Epilegomena §4, selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.
representative_people.works: Critique of Pure Reason; Dilthey’s Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883) as a documented reworking

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.

representative_people.context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.

representative_people.context: Language use and rule-following supply questions about intelligible action. This selection identifies a conceptual resource; particular historical reception is documented separately through Skinner and Geertz.

representative_people.context: Distinguishes conceptual errors, competent performances and what an act accomplishes. This is a resource for discussing explanations of action, not proof that every historical philosopher borrowed from him.

philhistory.scope_note: Covering laws, understanding action, historical facts, and objectivity are different disputes; participants do not form a shared school. Hempel’s probabilistic sketches, Dray’s challenge, Carr’s reciprocal research and Mink’s comprehension are distinct. Primary readings and publisher-only contexts are explicitly separated.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction
strands.focus: Elton’s research/writing/teaching agenda and Skinner’s apprenticeship reading identify practices of training.

strands.title: Narrative comprehension and truth
strands.focus: Mink separates grasping relations from truth tests and disputes both Gallie’s following and Hardy’s lived-narrative account.

strands.title: Knowledge of the past and speculative historical systems
strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.
intellectualhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Arthur O. Lovejoy: The Great Chain of Being (1936); Quentin Skinner: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); J. G. A. Pocock: “The history of political thought” (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975); Annabel S. Brett: Liberty, Right and Nature (1997); Reinhart Koselleck: Futures Past (German 1979; English 1985); Dominick LaCapra: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); John E. Toews: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987); Robert Darnton: The Business of Enlightenment (1979); Masao Maruyama: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–1944; English 1974); Mikiso Hane: English translation of Maruyama’s Studies (1974).

intellectualhistory.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

strands.title: History of ideas and recurring concepts
strands.focus: Lovejoy follows changing combinations of ideas across philosophical, religious and literary materials.

strands.title: Arguments, languages and historical action
strands.focus: Skinner, Pocock and Brett pursue distinct contextual inquiries; they are not interchangeable statements of one method.

strands.title: Conceptual change and historical time
strands.focus: Koselleck relates semantic change to social history without making concepts and social structures identical.

strands.title: Texts, contexts and experience
strands.focus: LaCapra develops textual criticism; Toews’s titled intervention marks a related debate whose detailed claims remain a reading task.

strands.title: Publishing and the circulation of ideas
strands.focus: Darnton connects thought with the material and commercial work of producing and distributing books. Chartier’s later studies follow texts’ mobility across attributions, printed versions, genres and translations, in his reviewers’ accounts.

strands.title: Japanese political thought and translation
strands.focus: Maruyama’s Tokugawa studies and Hane’s translation widen the selection while leaving its modernization interpretation open to scrutiny.
strands.works: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (English 1974)
